request.system: You are a sceptical results reviewer. Task: rank Medicare providers for audit. Each of 5,410 providers carries a PotentialFraud label (9.35% flagged) whose origin is undocumented; treat it as suspicion, not confirmed fraud. Claims run 27 Nov 2008 to 31 Dec 2009. The primary metric is PR-AUC; the audit queue holds about 100 providers. Pick the configuration to carry forward. Prefer a simpler model unless a more complex one is better by more than one standard deviation of PR-AUC across folds. Flag any result that looks too good. You may request up to 1 more round(s) of experiments; set stop=true if further search is unlikely to help. Rate your confidence in chosen_run (0-1): 1.0 means results are clear-cut and no reasonable reviewer would disagree; 0.5 means the top configs are too close to call or something looks off. (Independent run 3.)

concerns: Best LightGBM (run 7, PR-AUC 0.743) beats the best simple model (logistic run 5, 0.6925) by about 0.05, which is less than one fold SD (~0.069 for LightGBM, ~0.057 for logistic). Under the simplicity rule this favors logistic.
Fold SDs of 0.06-0.08 are large relative to the gaps between configs. Run 7 vs run 1 (0.743 vs 0.735) and most other differences are noise. Ranking among configs is not reliable.

ROC-AUC of 0.94-0.946 is very high and nearly identical across all model families and feature sets. That suggests the label is largely driven by a few strong, possibly volume-related or leaky features, or that the label is itself a rule-derived proxy. The label origin is undocumented, so the model may reproduce the labeling process rather than detect fraud.

Precision@50 of 0.74-0.79 is high for a 9.35% base rate. Combined with the high ROC-AUC it looks too good, so leakage should be checked: features aggregated over the whole claim window, provider-level aggregates built before the CV split, and duplicated or near-duplicate providers across folds.
Dropping size features (no_size) costs only 0.01-0.02 PR-AUC. This suggests the signal is not just provider size, but the differences are within noise.
Only about 500 positive providers are in the data, and the audit queue is about 100. Precision at k=100 was not reported, and the p@50 gap between models (0.74-0.79) is about 2-3 providers.
Claims cover about 13 months from a single period, so temporal generalization is untested. CV is probably random rather than time-based.
Flagged providers are suspicion labels, not confirmed fraud. Precision here measures agreement with the label, not audit yield.
